translations.title: Türkiye'den Laredo'ya Ürün Getirme: Hava, Deniz Ve Konsolidasyon
translations.excerpt: Türkiye'den ABD'ye mal getirmenin üç yolu var, ama asıl mesele hangisi değil. Asıl mesele malın iki ayrı gümrükten geçecek olması ve bunu nasıl yöneteceğin.
translations.coverAlt: Container ship being unloaded at a port terminal with cranes, photographic, no text
translations.metaTitle: Türkiye'den Laredo Deposuna Ürün Getirmenin Üç Yolu
translations.metaDescription: Türkiye'den Laredo depoya ürün nasıl gelir? Hava ve deniz seçenekleri, iç taşıma ve en kritik nokta: gümrüğü iki kez ödememenin yolu.
translations.content:
Türkiye'den Laredo'ya mal hava veya deniz yoluyla gelir; deniz genelde Houston gibi Körfez limanlarına, oradan karayoluyla Laredo'ya. Kritik nokta şu: mal ABD'ye girerken bir gümrük işlemi, Meksika'ya geçerken ikinci bir gümrük işlemi görür. Mal ABD'de satılmayacaksa bonded depo veya serbest bölge bu iki katmanı yönetmenin yoludur.

  • Türkiye'den ABD'ye üç yol var: hava kargo, deniz konteyneri (LCL veya FCL) ve küçük gönderiler için kurye.
  • Deniz yükü genelde Körfez limanlarına gelir ve oradan karayoluyla Laredo'ya taşınır.
  • Mal ABD'ye girerken ABD ithalat işlemi, Meksika'ya geçerken ayrı bir Meksika ithalatı görür.
  • Bonded depoda ABD gümrük vergisi ertelenir; serbest bölgede mal henüz ithal edilmiş sayılmaz.
  • Türkiye menşeli mal T-MEC kapsamında değildir, dolayısıyla Meksika'ya girişte tercihli tarifeden yararlanmaz.

Türkiye'den Laredo depoya ürün nasıl gelir?

Hava veya deniz yoluyla. Hava hızlı ve pahalı, deniz yavaş ve ucuz. Deniz yükü genelde Körfez limanlarına gelir, oradan karayoluyla Laredo'ya çekilir. Küçük gönderiler için kurye de var ama düzenli hacimde birim maliyeti yüksektir.

Türkiye'den Laredo'ya doğrudan bir hat yok, çünkü Laredo bir liman değil kara sınır kapısı. Mal önce ABD'ye giriyor, sonra karayoluyla Laredo'ya çekiliyor. Bunun üç yolu var ve seçim büyük ölçüde aciliyet ile hacim arasındaki dengeye bakıyor. Hava kargo en hızlısı: mal Türkiye'den bir ABD havalimanına uçuyor, gümrükleniyor ve karayoluyla Laredo'ya geliyor. Numune, ilk parti, sezon yakalama ve yüksek değerli küçük hacimli ürünlerde mantıklı, ama kilogram başına maliyet denizin katları olduğu için düzenli hacimde sürdürülebilir değil. Deniz yolu düzenli hacmin standardı: mal konteynerle Körfez veya Doğu Kıyısı limanlarına geliyor, orada gümrükleniyor ve karayoluyla Laredo'ya taşınıyor. Houston gibi Körfez limanları Laredo'ya en yakın seçenek olduğu için iç taşıma bacağını kısaltıyor. Deniz tarafında iki alt seçenek var: tam konteyner, yani FCL, ve parsiyel, yani LCL. Hacmin bir konteyneri doldurmuyorsa LCL ile başlarsın; doldurmaya yaklaştığında FCL genelde birim başına daha ucuza gelir. Üçüncü yol kurye, ki numune ve çok küçük gönderiler dışında düzenli iş için uygun değil, çünkü her paket ayrı gümrük görür ve birim maliyet hızla yükselir.

En kritik nokta: mal iki gümrükten geçiyor

Türkiye'den gelen mal ABD'ye girerken bir ithalat, Meksika'ya geçerken ikinci bir ithalat görüyor. Mal ABD'de satılmayacaksa, ABD gümrük vergisini kalıcı olarak ödemek gereksiz maliyet olabilir. Bonded depo ve serbest bölge tam bu durum için var.

Bu, Türkiye'den mal getirip Meksika'ya satan herkesin bilmesi gereken ve çoğu içerikte hiç geçmeyen nokta. Malın rotası Türkiye'den Meksika'ya ABD üzerinden geçtiğinde, iki ayrı ülkenin gümrüğüyle iki ayrı kez muhatap oluyorsun. Birincisi ABD'ye giriş: mal ABD'ye ithal ediliyor, sınıflandırılıyor ve Türkiye menşeli olduğu için ABD'nin genel tarife rejimine tabi oluyor. İkincisi Meksika'ya giriş: mal sınırdan geçerken Meksika ithalatı yapılıyor ve orada da Türkiye menşeli olduğu için T-MEC tercihli tarifesinden yararlanamıyor. Yani iki kez gümrük, iki kez evrak. Şimdi asıl soru: malı ABD'de satmayacaksan, ABD gümrük vergisini kalıcı olarak ödemenin bir anlamı var mı? Çoğu durumda yok, ve mevzuat bunun için iki araç sunuyor. Bonded depoda mal ABD gümrük denetimi altında tutulur ve ithalat vergisi mal oradan çıkana kadar ertelenir; mal yeniden ihraç edilirse, yani Meksika'ya gönderilirse, o vergi yükü farklı işler. Serbest bölgede ise mal henüz ABD'ye ithal edilmiş sayılmaz, dolayısıyla oradan Meksika'ya çıkan mal ABD gümrük vergisini hiç doğurmayabilir; ayrıca serbest bölgede etiketleme, kitleme ve montaj gibi katma değerli işlemler yapılabilir. Hangi aracın senin durumuna uyduğu ürüne, hacme ve ne kadar süre bekleteceğine bağlı, o yüzden bunu gümrük müşavirinle konuşmadan rota kurma.

Laredo'da ne yapılır?

Konsolidasyon, hazırlık ve tek ithalat. Farklı tedarikçilerden gelen mal burada birleşir, İspanyolca NOM etiketi vurulur, belgeler hazırlanır ve tek pedimentoyla Meksika'ya geçer. Böylece Meksika tarafındaki sabit maliyetler bölünür.

Laredo'nun rolü bir ara durak olmaktan fazlası; asıl işin yapıldığı yer. Mal buraya ulaştığında dört şey oluyor. Birincisi teslim alma ve sayım: Türkiye'den gelen sevkiyat kontrol ediliyor, eksik veya hasar varsa kaynağa dönmeden tespit ediliyor. İkincisi konsolidasyon: birden fazla tedarikçiden veya birden fazla sevkiyattan gelen mal tek bir ithalat partisinde birleştiriliyor. Bunun neden önemli olduğunu daha önce de yazdık ama tekrar etmeye değer: Meksika tarafındaki sabit maliyetler, yani gümrük müşaviri ücreti, prevalidasyon ve işlem harcı, pedimento başına ödeniyor. Dört ayrı küçük ithalat yapmak yerine tek ithalat yapmak, aynı sabit maliyeti dört kat mala bölüyor. Üçüncüsü hazırlık: Meksika'ya girecek malın İspanyolca NOM etiketi burada vuruluyor, çünkü etiketi menşede veya sınırda basmak, Meksika'da parça başına etiketlemekten her zaman ucuz. Dördüncüsü belge: fatura, çeki listesi ve beyan edilen değer birbiriyle tutarlı hâle getiriliyor, çünkü gümrükte takılmaların çoğu mesafeden değil tutarsız evraktan kaynaklanıyor. Bu dördü tamamlandığında mal tek pedimentoyla geçiyor ve iyi belgelenmiş bir sevkiyat Monterrey'e 1-2 iş gününde ulaşıyor. BringGo Ship'in Laredo deposu tam olarak bu işlevi görüyor, Monterrey deposu da Meksika içi teslimatı ve iadeleri karşılıyor.

Sık sorulan sorular

Türkiye'den Laredo'ya doğrudan gönderim var mı?

Doğrudan yok, çünkü Laredo bir liman değil kara sınır kapısı. Mal önce hava veya deniz yoluyla ABD'ye giriyor, gümrükleniyor ve karayoluyla Laredo'ya çekiliyor. Deniz yükünde Houston gibi Körfez limanları Laredo'ya en yakın seçenek olduğu için iç taşıma bacağını kısaltıyor.

Hava mı deniz mi seçmeliyim?

Aciliyet ve hacme bakın. Hava numune, ilk parti, sezon yakalama ve yüksek değerli küçük hacimli üründe mantıklı ama kilogram maliyeti denizin katları. Düzenli hacimde deniz standarttır; konteyneri dolduramıyorsanız LCL ile başlayıp hacim büyüdükçe FCL'e geçmek genelde en ucuz yoldur.

Malım kaç kez gümrükten geçiyor?

İki kez. Bir kez ABD'ye girerken, bir kez Meksika'ya geçerken. Türkiye menşeli mal her iki tarafta da tercihli tarifeden yararlanmaz, çünkü Türkiye'nin ne ABD ile bu kapsamda ne Meksika ile yürürlükte bir serbest ticaret anlaşması var. Bu, rota maliyetini hesaplarken en çok atlanan kalem.

ABD gümrük vergisini ödememem mümkün mü?

Mal ABD'de satılmayacaksa mevzuat iki araç sunuyor. Bonded depoda ithalat vergisi mal çıkana kadar ertelenir. Serbest bölgede mal henüz ABD'ye ithal edilmiş sayılmaz, dolayısıyla oradan Meksika'ya çıkan malda ABD vergisi hiç doğmayabilir. Hangisinin uygun olduğunu gümrük müşavirinle netleştir.

Laredo'da ne yapılıyor?

Teslim alma ve sayım, konsolidasyon, İspanyolca NOM etiketleme ve belge hazırlığı. Konsolidasyon en değerli kısmı: Meksika tarafındaki sabit maliyetler pedimento başına ödendiği için, birden fazla sevkiyatı tek ithalatta birleştirmek birim maliyeti belirgin şekilde düşürüyor.

translations.title: US To Mexico Freight Forwarder: What They Do And What They Do Not
translations.excerpt: Freight forwarder, customs broker, 3PL: three different roles that get used interchangeably. Knowing which one you actually need is what stops your freight sitting at the border.
translations.coverAlt: Logistics coordinator reviewing shipment documents in a warehouse office, photographic, no text
translations.metaTitle: US to Mexico Freight Forwarder: What They Do and Do Not Do
translations.metaDescription: A freight forwarder arranges transport but does not clear your goods. Who does what between forwarder, customs broker and cross-border 3PL, and which you need.
translations.content:
A freight forwarder arranges and coordinates transport but does not clear goods through customs. In Mexico only a licensed customs broker can file the pedimento. A cross-border 3PL combines both plus warehousing and delivery, which is why most shippers moving goods between the US and Mexico end up needing more than a forwarder alone.

  • A freight forwarder arranges transport and documentation but does not itself clear goods through customs.
  • In Mexico only a licensed customs broker, an agente aduanal with a patente, can file the pedimento (SAT).
  • A cross-border 3PL combines forwarding, clearance, warehousing and final delivery under one accountable party.
  • Trucking carries roughly 73 to 74 percent of US Mexico trade, so most freight in this lane moves by road (WorldCity, Census).
  • A well documented truck reaches Monterrey from Laredo in one to two business days (operational data).

What does a freight forwarder actually do?

Arranges transport. A forwarder books capacity, coordinates carriers, prepares transport documentation and tracks the shipment. What a forwarder does not do is clear your goods through Mexican customs, because that requires a separate license.

The term freight forwarder gets used as a catch all for anyone who moves goods internationally, which is why so many shippers end up with the wrong provider for their situation. A forwarder is an organiser of transport. They book capacity with carriers, coordinate the legs of a journey, prepare and manage transport documentation, consolidate shipments where that makes sense, and give you visibility over where your goods are. For a shipment moving from Asia to the United States, a competent forwarder may be all you need, because they handle the movement and a customs broker on the US side handles the entry. The US to Mexico lane works differently and this is where the confusion costs money. Mexico requires that the customs declaration, the pedimento, be filed by a licensed Mexican customs broker holding a patente. A freight forwarder, however capable, cannot do this unless they also hold that license or work with someone who does. So when a forwarder quotes you a rate to Mexico, the honest question to ask is what happens at the border: do they clear the goods themselves, do they hand off to a broker they work with, or do they hand off to you. Those three answers describe very different services, and the third one is where shipments sit while someone works out who is responsible.

Forwarder, customs broker or 3PL: which do you need?

A forwarder if you only need transport arranged and you already have clearance covered. A customs broker if you have transport handled and need the pedimento filed. A cross-border 3PL if you want one party accountable from pickup to final delivery, which is most shippers.

The three roles are complementary rather than competing, and picking correctly is a matter of what you already have covered. A freight forwarder is right when your constraint is capacity and coordination: you know how to clear goods in Mexico, you have a broker, and you need someone to organize the movement. A customs broker is right when your constraint is compliance: your transport is arranged, perhaps by your buyer or an existing carrier, and what you need is the entry filed correctly. Note that in Mexico this is not optional for commercial imports, so you will need a broker in some form regardless. A cross-border 3PL is right when your constraint is that you do not want to manage the border at all. This kind of operator combines the forwarder role, the customs broker role, warehousing on one or both sides, and final delivery, under a single accountable party. Most companies shipping regularly between the US and Mexico converge on this because of what the alternative looks like in practice: three providers, each responsible for their own leg, and a handoff at the border where a problem belongs to nobody. Since trucking carries roughly three quarters of US Mexico trade, most of this happens by road, where handoffs are physical: a trailer waits while the next party accepts responsibility for it.

What to ask before you choose

Ask who files the pedimento, whether they have warehouses on both sides, whether they can label and prepare goods before crossing, and whether you get one invoice and one contact. The answers separate a coordinator from an operator.

Four questions do most of the work in separating providers, and they can be asked in a single email. First, who files the pedimento? If they can name the licensed broker, you are talking to an operator who knows the lane. If the answer is vague, that can still work but ask how the handoff works and who is accountable if it goes wrong. If the answer is that you need to arrange it, you are buying transport only, and you should price the missing piece before comparing quotes. Second, do you have warehouses on both sides of the border? This determines whether they can consolidate before the crossing, which is where the customs cost per unit falls, and whether they can hold and deliver inside Mexico afterwards. Third, can you prepare goods before crossing? Spanish NOM labelling has to happen before goods are offered for sale in Mexico, and doing it at a border warehouse is far cheaper than relabelling per unit after arrival. Fourth, do I get one invoice and one point of contact? This sounds like a convenience question and it is really an accountability question: when responsibility is split across three companies, the gaps between them are where shipments stall. As for transit itself, that is rarely the differentiator. A well documented truck reaches Monterrey from Laredo in one to two business days regardless of who booked it. What differs between providers is what happens in the hours around the border, not on the highway. BringGo Ship operates warehouses in Laredo and Monterrey on the same lane, which is the profile these four questions are designed to find.

Who does what on the US Mexico lane

RoleArranges transportFiles the pedimento
Freight forwarderYesNo, unless licensed or partnered
Mexican customs brokerNoYes, exclusively
Cross-border 3PLYesCoordinated with a licensed broker
Warehousing both sidesForwarder rarely3PL typically
Spanish NOM labellingRarely3PL at the border
Single accountable partyNo3PL, one invoice one contact

Definitions

  • Freight forwarder: A freight forwarder arranges and coordinates transport and documentation but does not itself clear goods through customs.
  • Customs broker: In Mexico a customs broker is the licensed professional who is the only party permitted to file the pedimento.
  • Cross-border 3PL: A cross-border 3PL combines forwarding, customs clearance, warehousing and delivery under a single accountable party.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between a freight forwarder and a customs broker?

A freight forwarder arranges transport, books capacity, prepares transport documentation and tracks the shipment. A customs broker files the customs declaration. In Mexico only a licensed customs broker with a patente can file the pedimento, so a forwarder alone cannot clear your goods into the country.

Do I need a freight forwarder for shipping to Mexico?

Only if you need transport arranged and coordinated. If you already have carriers and a broker, you may not. What you cannot skip for a commercial import is the licensed Mexican customs broker, because the pedimento can only be filed by one. Most regular shippers use a cross-border 3PL that covers both roles.

Can a US freight forwarder clear my goods into Mexico?

Not by themselves. Mexican clearance requires a licensed Mexican customs broker. A US forwarder may work with one, which is a normal arrangement, but ask specifically how the handoff works and who is accountable if something goes wrong at the border. If they say you need to arrange clearance, you are buying transport only.

What should I ask a provider before choosing?

Who files the pedimento, whether they have warehouses on both sides of the border, whether they can apply Spanish NOM labelling before crossing, and whether you get one invoice and one point of contact. These four answers separate a transport coordinator from an operator who owns the border.

Does the choice affect how fast my freight arrives?

Less than people expect on the road, more than people expect at the border. A well documented truck reaches Monterrey from Laredo in one to two business days regardless of who booked it. What differs is what happens in the hours around the crossing, where incomplete documentation and unclear responsibility cause the delays.

translations.title: When To Split Inventory Between A US And A Mexican Warehouse, And When To Keep One Pool
translations.excerpt: Splitting stock across the border is a network decision, not a storage decision. Here is the per-product test, the hidden costs, and the signal to consolidate again.
translations.coverAlt: Dark mode schematic of two warehouse nodes, one in Texas and one in northern Mexico, connected by a single flow line, wi
translations.metaTitle: When To Split Inventory Between US And Mexico Warehouses
translations.metaDescription: A split inventory buys delivery speed and costs you flexibility. Here is how to decide per product, what the split really costs, and when to collapse back to one pool.
keywords: split inventory us and mexico warehouse
translations.content:
Split inventory when a product's Mexican demand is steady enough to predict and its stockout cost is high. Keep one pool when demand is thin, seasonal or new, because a split halves your flexibility on both sides. The deciding variable is predictability per product, not total volume.

  • A split trades flexibility for delivery speed, and both sides of that trade are real.
  • The unit of the decision is the product, not the company; most catalogs should be split partially.
  • Units placed on the Mexican side are committed, because repositioning them back is rarely economic.
  • A split multiplies the number of places a forecast can be wrong.
  • Consolidating back to one pool is a legitimate move, not an admission of failure.

When Does Splitting Inventory Actually Pay Off?

When local delivery speed changes conversion or account health, and the product's demand is predictable enough to commit units in advance.

Holding stock on the Mexican side buys one thing: distance already covered. The order ships from Monterrey instead of waiting on a border crossing, so the customer sees a shorter promise and your listing carries a local dispatch. That is worth real money when it changes whether people buy, and worth very little when it does not. So the first test is commercial. Does the delivery promise move your conversion rate on this product? For competitive categories with domestic alternatives, it usually does, because the buyer is comparing your dispatch estimate against a seller who already has stock in the country. For niche products with no local substitute, buyers are more patient and the premium for local stock shrinks. The second test is about account signals. Marketplace accounts respond to late shipments and to cancellations, and a longer, more variable fulfillment path produces more of both. If your account health metrics are being dragged down by the tail of slow orders rather than by the average, forward stocking attacks exactly that tail. This is often a stronger argument than the conversion one, because account damage spreads to your entire catalog. The third test is predictability, and it is the one that disqualifies most products. Committing units to the Mexican side means committing to a demand estimate weeks in advance, with no cheap way to change your mind. A product with a stable weekly sales rate can absorb that commitment. A product that sells in unpredictable bursts cannot, because you will either starve it or strand inventory that has to be discounted to move. Put the three together and the pattern is clear. Split the products where speed changes the sale, where the slow tail is hurting your account, and where you can defend a demand number. Everything else stays in one pool and ships when ordered. Most sellers who split their entire catalog at once end up reversing part of the decision within a year, having paid for the lesson in dead stock rather than in analysis.

Which Products Belong on the Mexican Side of the Border?

Fast, stable, high-margin products with local competition belong in Mexico; new, seasonal, bulky or unproven products belong upstream.

Rank the catalog before you decide anything. Sort by units sold and look at the top group, then check how stable each of those products has been week to week. Volume alone is misleading, because a product can rack up units in irregular bursts. What you want is volume plus rhythm, and the products that have both are your split candidates. Margin sets the tolerance for error. A high-margin product can carry the extra cost of forward stocking and still profit, and if you overshoot the quantity, the discount needed to clear it does not erase the year. A thin-margin product has no room for either mistake, so it should stay in the pool that keeps options open. Physical characteristics matter more than sellers expect. Bulky items consume storage in proportion to their volume, so committing them to the Mexican side ties up space that a smaller, faster product could have used. Fragile items add handling risk at each additional touch. High-value items concentrate loss risk in one location. None of these are automatic disqualifiers, but each one raises the bar the product has to clear. Return behavior belongs in the decision too. Products with heavy returns generate a reverse flow that has to land somewhere, and a Mexican location that can receive, inspect and restock them locally is a genuine advantage. For those categories, the split is justified by the return side even when the outbound argument is only moderate. Ignoring returns is how sellers end up with a fast outbound network and a slow, expensive way back. Finally, treat new products as ineligible by default. Without a demand history, a forward placement is a guess with a long correction cycle. Sell them from the pool first, gather several weeks of clean data, then promote the ones that earn it. Promotion should be a routine review, not a one-time architecture decision, because the products that deserve local stock change as the catalog matures.

What Does a Split Cost You That a Single Pool Does Not?

It costs flexibility, adds a second forecast to get wrong, and creates two places where the same product can be simultaneously short and long.

The obvious costs are the ones sellers plan for: an extra storage location, an extra receiving process, more movement. Those are visible and manageable. The costs that hurt are the ones that do not appear on an invoice. The first is pooled variance. One inventory location absorbs demand shocks better than two locations holding the same total units, because a surge in one channel can be served from the same pile that serves the other. Split the pile and each half faces demand on its own. This is why a split often needs more total inventory to deliver the same service level, and that increase is a permanent working capital cost, not a one-time setup. The second is commitment. Units on the Mexican side are effectively spent. Moving them back is possible but rarely worth the freight and handling, so a forecasting error becomes a discount instead of a transfer. In a single pool, the same error is just a delay. This asymmetry is the strongest argument for splitting slowly and per product. The third is operational surface area. Two locations mean two sets of counts to reconcile, two receiving procedures to keep accurate, and one more place where a channel listing can point at inventory that is not there. Overselling risk grows because the number of moving parts grows. This is manageable with good sync rules, but it is not free, and the effort lands on the same small team. The fourth is attention. Every location added is a place someone has to look at every week. Small teams underestimate this, and the symptom is a slow drift into stale counts and forgotten aging stock. Before adding a location, ask who owns it operationally, by name. If the honest answer is that everyone will keep an eye on it, the split will quietly degrade until someone notices a large write-off.

How Do You Decide the Split Ratio Without a Forecast You Trust?

Start from the cover period you are willing to commit locally, not from a percentage of total stock.

Percentages are the wrong frame. Deciding to keep some share of inventory in Mexico sounds concrete but has no logic behind it, and it produces the same ratio for a product that sells daily and one that sells monthly. The useful frame is time: how many days of local sales do you want the Mexican location to be able to cover on its own? Answer that per product, then convert. Take the daily sales rate you can defend for that product in Mexico, multiply by the cover period you chose, and that is the quantity to place locally. Everything else stays upstream. This automatically gives fast products more units and slow products fewer, which is exactly what you want, and it does so without anyone arguing about a percentage. Choose the cover period from your replenishment reality. It should comfortably exceed the time it takes to get more units into the Mexican warehouse, because the whole point is to not go dark while a restock is in motion. If your replenishment cycle is long and variable, the cover period grows, and if that number starts to look uncomfortable, the honest conclusion may be that this product should not be split at all. When the demand estimate is weak, shorten the commitment instead of guessing harder. Place a smaller local quantity, watch how fast it depletes, and adjust on the next cycle. Two conservative cycles produce better information than one confident one, and they cost far less when the estimate turns out wrong. This is the same logic as sizing a first order for a new market: buy information before buying volume. Review the ratio on a schedule and on triggers. Seasons change the daily rate, promotions change it temporarily, and product lifecycles change it permanently. A local placement that made sense at launch can be badly wrong two quarters later, and nothing in the system will tell you unless someone looks. Put the review on the calendar with the products listed, so the answer is data rather than memory.

When Should You Collapse Back to One Pool?

When the local stock stops turning, when demand becomes erratic, or when the split is consuming more attention than it returns.

Consolidation gets treated as a retreat, which is why sellers hold split networks long after they stopped paying. The correct view is that network shape is a variable, and moving it in either direction is normal management. Define in advance what would make you reverse the decision, because that is much easier to do calmly than in the middle of a cash squeeze. The clearest signal is turn rate. If a product's local stock keeps aging past its own replenishment cycle, the local placement is not being used, it is being stored. Storage without turnover is the exact cost the split was supposed to buy speed with, and speed nobody is consuming is not worth paying for. The second signal is erratic demand. Products drift. A steady seller can become lumpy when a competitor changes price, when a channel changes its ranking behavior, or when the product simply matures. Once the weekly pattern stops being predictable, the argument for committing units locally weakens, and the pool becomes the better home again. The third signal is operational strain. If reconciliations keep failing, if counts drift between locations, or if the team is spending its week chasing where units are rather than selling them, the network is more complex than the organization can carry. Simplifying is a legitimate fix. A smaller, well-run network beats a larger one that nobody has time to maintain. Collapsing back should be planned, not abrupt. Stop replenishing the local position, let it sell down rather than paying to move it, keep the channel promises accurate as the local availability shrinks, and switch the listings to the pooled fulfillment path before the last local units go. Done this way, consolidation costs almost nothing and leaves you with something valuable: a documented reason, so that when the product stabilizes again you know exactly what to watch for before splitting a second time.

One Inventory Pool vs a Split Across Two Warehouses

DimensionSingle poolSplit across US and Mexico
Delivery promise to Mexican buyersLonger and more variableShorter and more consistent for stocked items
Flexibility after a forecast errorHigh, units are not committedLow, repositioning is rarely economic
Total inventory needed for the same service levelLower, variance is pooledHigher, each side faces demand alone
Return handling in MexicoReverse flow travels furtherCan be received and restocked locally
Operational overheadOne count, one processTwo counts, two processes, more sync risk
Best suited toNew, seasonal, bulky or erratic productsFast, stable, high-margin products with local competition

How BringGo Ship Fits a Split or Pooled Setup

We operate a warehouse in Laredo, Texas and a warehouse in Monterrey, Mexico, and we move seller inventory from the US side to the Mexican side on that route. That means you can hold everything in Laredo and ship as orders come in, hold a forward position in Monterrey for the products that earn it, or run both at once and change the balance later. We receive, count and store the goods, we pick and dispatch from whichever side you choose, and we process returns that land in Monterrey so those units can be inspected and put back into sellable stock locally. Our team supports you in English, Spanish and Turkish. You choose which products move forward, since that turns on your margins and your demand history, and we supply the lane timings and the per shipment receipt data those choices need. What we do is run both positions and give you the movement records so the split ratio is a decision you revisit with evidence.

Definitions

  • Inventory pooling: Holding stock in one location so that demand variability from several channels is absorbed by the same units.
  • Forward stocking: Placing inventory close to the customer in advance of demand in order to shorten the delivery promise.
  • Cover period: The number of days of expected local sales that a forward position is sized to support on its own.
  • Repositioning: Moving inventory back from a forward location to a central one, usually expensive enough that forward placement is treated as a commitment.

Frequently asked questions

Should a new seller split inventory immediately?

Rarely. Without demand history per product, a forward placement is a guess with a slow correction cycle. Sell from one pool first, collect several clean weeks of data, then move only the products that show stable demand and a delivery-sensitive category.

Does splitting inventory always shorten delivery times?

Only for the units actually held locally. Orders for products that were not placed forward still travel the full path, so a partial split produces a mixed customer experience. Set channel handling expectations per product rather than promising one speed for the whole catalog.

How does a split change my safety stock?

It usually increases the total. Two locations each face demand on their own, so the variance that a single pool absorbed now has to be covered twice. Size the buffer separately for each position rather than dividing your existing number in half.

Can I move stock back from Mexico to the US if I over-commit?

It is possible but rarely economic once freight and handling are counted, which is why forward placement should be treated as a commitment. In practice, most sellers clear an over-commitment through pricing and promotion in Mexico rather than by moving units back.

What is the simplest first step toward a split?

Pick your two or three most stable, highest-margin products, place a short cover period of each in Mexico, and measure two things: how fast the local stock depletes and whether the shorter delivery promise changed conversion. That test costs little and answers the question with your own data.
